title: Women entrepreneurs could benefit from better targeting, without changing the program content[
gist: A World Bank working paper pooling experiments with 2,595 entrepreneurs in Uganda, South Africa and Mexico finds business upgrading programs yield zero average returns for women, but targeting women in the top quartile of a 100-point Program Readiness Scorecard (score of at least 61) produces returns identical to men's, recouping program costs in about four months.

insights.claim: Pooled experimental data from 2,595 entrepreneurs in Uganda, South Africa and Mexico show male entrepreneurs gain significantly from business upgrading programs while women's average gains are statistically indistinguishable from zero.
insights.so_what: Billions in untargeted SME support yield poor returns for half the participants.
insights.quote: Without any targeting, male entrepreneurs who receive business upgrading support show large, statistically significant gains in firm performance.
insights.locator: The Gap — And What Causes It
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Typical business upgrading programs cost around US$758 per participant.
insights.so_what: Benchmark cost for evaluating SME training ROI.
insights.locator: The Gap — And What Causes It
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The standard policy response to weak returns for women, adding gender-specific content, women-only programs or quotas, is argued to be less cost-effective than better selection and targeting.
insights.so_what: Shifts development spending from program redesign to screening tools.
insights.quote: Business upgrading programs are not necessarily broken for women. The selection and targeting process could be tailored to improve their efficacy.
insights.locator: A new World Bank working paper
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The Program Readiness Scorecard is a 100-point composite of ten observable behaviors (the '10 Es') covering credit constraints, baseline business skills and growth attitudes, and deliberately excludes current profits and firm size.
insights.so_what: A field-deployable screen for SME growth potential that avoids selecting already-successful firms.
insights.quote: Crucially, it does not use current profits or firm size, avoiding the trap of screening already-successful firms.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Applying the PRS as a gender-neutral screen makes women's returns statistically significant, but men's returns remain roughly twice as large.
insights.so_what: Neutral screens narrow but do not close gaps when underlying distributions differ.
insights.quote: But men's returns remain roughly twice as large. The gap narrows; it does not close.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Men average 55.2 on the PRS versus 51.4 for women, which the authors attribute to structural barriers limiting women's access to capital, managerial experience and networks rather than innate ability.
insights.so_what: Readiness gaps stem from capital and network access, pointing to where interventions should focus.
insights.quote: Men average 55.2 on the PRS; women average 51.4
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Women in the top quartile of the female PRS distribution (score of at least 61) achieve treatment effects virtually identical to the average man, a difference of 0.013 SD (p=0.892), while women below the threshold show no returns.
insights.so_what: The gender program gap is a selection problem, solvable with targeted screening.
insights.quote: The difference in returns between Average Men and High-PRS Women is 0.013 SD (p=0.892).
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: High-readiness women entrepreneurs recoup the cost of a typical business upgrading program in roughly four months through profit gains, the same as men, making them an under-served commercial market for private business development and consulting firms.
insights.so_what: Identifies a profitable, overlooked customer segment for private SME service providers in emerging markets.
insights.quote: High-readiness women, for example, recoup the cost of a typical program within roughly four months through profit gains — the same timeframe as men.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The authors propose development finance institutions use the PRS as an investment screen for pipeline selection in value-chain integration, investment-readiness programs or SME lending, directing capital toward women-led firms currently passed over.
insights.so_what: Could reshape how DFIs and SME lenders underwrite small firms, expanding women-led firm lending.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The authors recommend a tiered approach: broad foundational support for many entrepreneurs and intensive upgrading only for those the PRS identifies as program-ready.
insights.so_what: More efficient allocation of SME support budgets.
insights.quote: broad foundational support for many, intensive upgrading for those who are ready, with the PRS serving as the gateway between the two.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
